## {data-state="hide-menubar"}


<h1> `prefviz` </h1>

<h2> A visualisation toolkit for preferential election data </h2>

<hr>

<h4> Linh Ngo, Dianne Cook, Damjan Vukcevic </h4>

![](../images/prefviz-sticker.png){.absolute top=295 left=750 width="30%"}

## Imagine you are the organiser of MelbURN, and you need to decide which catering to order for your next event...

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
So you make a list of catering options, and go out to ask every attendee to rank their preference from most to least preferred.

1. Pizza
2. Spring roll
3. Sushi
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment}
After everyone has made their choice, your data looks like this:

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Define the people and catering options
people <- c("Alice", "Ben", "Carla", "David", "Ella")
foods <- c("pizza", "spring roll", "sushi")

# Create the tibble with random rankings for illustration
set.seed(123)  # for reproducibility

df <- expand.grid(name = people, food_type = foods) %>%
  group_by(name) %>%
  mutate(rank = sample(1:3, size = length(foods), replace = FALSE)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  as_tibble()

df
```

:::
:::

::::

## You decided to look into people's first choice

::: {..fragment}
`dop_irv()` does some slight transformation, ...

```{r}
irv_tbl <- df |>
  long_preferences(
    ballot,
    id_cols = name,
    item_col = food_type,
    rank_col = rank
  ) |>
  dop_irv(preferences_col = ballot, value_type = "percentage")

irv_tbl |>
  filter(round == 1) |>
  select(-round, -winner) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

:::

::: {.fragment}
Which `dop_bar()` visualizes directly as a bar chart
```{r}
dop_bar(irv_tbl, items = -c(round, winner), at_round = 1)
```

:::

## Alternatively, you look at pairwise comparisons

If we pick any 2 catering options and see which one people ranked higher on their ballot, who wins?

```{r}
prefs_tbl <- df |>
  long_preferences(
    ballot,
    id_cols = name,
    item_col = food_type,
    rank_col = rank
  )

pw_result <- pairwise_calculator(prefs_tbl, preferences_col = ballot)

pairwise_heatmap(pw_result, value = "tcp")
```

*Each cell shows the proportion of ballots that preferred the row option over the column option.*

## But what if you run this poll across every event MelbURN has ever hosted?

I don't know how many events MelbURN has hosted, but assume 150 events 😬😬😬

This is not `prefviz` code, because `prefviz` has a better solution.

```{r}
#| fig.width: 6
#| fig-align: center

set.seed(42)
n_events <- 150

# Generate 150 event compositions (same diverse patterns as 4-event example)
composition_tbl <- tibble(
  event = paste0("Event_", 1:n_events),
  pizza = runif(n_events, 0.05, 0.80),
  `spring roll` = runif(n_events, 0.05, 0.80),
  sushi = 1 - pizza - `spring roll`
) %>%
  mutate(across(pizza:`spring roll`, ~ pmax(pmin(., 0.90), 0.05))) %>%
  mutate(sushi = 1 - pizza - `spring roll`) |>
  filter(sushi > 0, pizza > 0, `spring roll` > 0)

# Same 4-event style plot, now for 150 events
composition_long <- composition_tbl %>%
  pivot_longer(-event, names_to = "food", values_to = "pct")

ggplot(composition_long, aes(x = event, y = pct, fill = food)) +
  geom_col(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(pct, accuracy = 1)),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("pizza" = "#E76F51",
                               "spring roll" = "#588157",
                               "sushi" = "#457B9D")) +
  labs(y = "Proportion", title = "Catering Preferences: 150 Events") +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 14, face = "bold"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, size = 3),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 6))
```

## Introduce: Ternary plot 🎉🎉🎉

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="65%"}

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

tern_food <- composition_tbl |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(top_choice = c("pizza", "spring roll", "sushi")[which.max(c_across(pizza:sushi))]) |>
  ungroup() |>
  as_ternable(items = pizza:sushi)

ggplot(get_tern_data2d(tern_food), aes(x = x1, y = x2)) +
  add_ternary_base() +
  geom_ternary_region(
    aes(fill = after_stat(vertex_labels)),
    vertex_labels = tern_food$vertex_labels,
    alpha = 0.3, color = NA, show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_point(aes(color = top_choice), alpha = 0.7, size = 4) +
  add_vertex_labels(tern_food$simplex_vertices) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("pizza" = "#E76F51", "spring roll" = "#588157", "sushi" = "#457B9D")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("pizza" = "#E76F51", "spring roll" = "#588157", "sushi" = "#457B9D"), name = "Top choice") +
  labs(title = "All 150 events at once") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 20, hjust = 0.5),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 14),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 16)
  )
```

*The same 150-event data from the last slide, now as a ternary plot — every event's full pizza/spring roll/sushi split is a single point.*
:::

::: {.column width="35%"}

**How to read this plot?**

::: {.incremental}
- The edges are the axes, running from 0 to 1
- Each point represents 1 observation (or stacked bar), and is made up of 3 parts: %pizza, %spring roll, and %sushi
- If the point sits at one of the vertices, it means 100% of the composition is that option.
- If the point sits in the center, it means equal compositions of all options (33% each)
:::

:::

::::

:::{.columns}

```{r}
#| echo: true

```

:::

```{r}
    aes(fill = after_stat(vertex_labels)), 
    vertex_labels = tern_2d$vertex_labels, 
    alpha = 0.3, color = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
```

:::

:::{.fragment fragment-index=4 .code-reveal}

```{r}
#| eval: false

```
:::

:::{.fragment fragment-index=5 .code-reveal}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
  geom_point(aes(color = true_winner))
```
:::

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

:::{.r-stack}
![](../images/layer1.png){.fragment fragment-index=2}

![](../images/layer2.png){.fragment fragment-index=3}

![](../images/layer3.png){.fragment fragment-index=4}

![](../images/layer4.png){.fragment fragment-index=5}
:::

:::

:::

::: {.notes}
- Each region is labelled by the party dominating that vertex: ALP (left), LNP (right), Other (top)
- Points near a vertex = strong first-preference vote for that party; central points = split across parties
- Most electorates cluster in the centre-left (ALP/LNP territory) — very few have a strong Other share
- Points coloured by the *winning* party, not the leading first-preference party
- Key observation: electorates in the Other region still end up electing ALP or LNP — but an ALP/LNP first-preference never flips to the other side
- Question for the audience: how does an electorate with a majority Other first preference end up with an ALP or LNP winner?
:::

## Code

```{r detourr-code}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: "1-3|5-6|8-15"

tern_hd <- as_ternable(
  pref25_hd_all |> filter(CountNumber == 0),
  items = c(ALP, LNP, GRN, IND, Other)
)

dtour_data <- get_tern_datahd(tern_hd) |>
  mutate(Winner = factor(coalesce(Winner, labels), levels = c("ALP", "LNP", "GRN", "IND", "Other")))

detour(
  dtour_data,
  tour_aes(projection = x1:x4, colour = Winner, labels = text)
) |>
  tour_path(planned_tour(lt), fps = 60) |>
  show_scatter(
    axes    = FALSE,
    palette = detour_colors,
    edges   = get_tern_edges(tern_hd),
    size    = 1
  )
```

:::
